newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe expects higher price for staple maize.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe expects higher price for staple maize.

text.p: Zimbabwe is likely to see higher prices for its staple maize crop after poor weather and disease slashed production, an industry official said on Tuesday.
"It's a bit difficult to assess at the moment but my belief is that maize is going to go up," said Zimbabwe Agricultural Commodities Exchange (ZIMACE) administrator Ian Goggin.

The food security unit of the 12-nation Southern African Development Community, of which Zimbabwe is a member, expects Zimbabwe's total maize production from the 1996/97 season to drop by 16 percent to 2.195 million tonnes due to heavy rains and grey leaf disease.
Goggin said he expected maize prices on ZIMACE to range between Z$1,300 and Z$1,400 a tonne in July from their current Z$1,240, possibly hitting Z$1,800 by the end of the marketing season next March.
Zimbabwe's Commercial Farmers Union (CFU) earlier this month urged maize growers to delay selling their crops until prices started picking up at the beginning of September.
Local wheat production, by contrast, was expected to rise.
But industry officials saw wheat prices rising on the back of reduced overall world production. Prices plunged last season due to high production levels worldwide.

"Argentina cut their production by 25 percent, Canada also reduced production and Australia harvested a record crop last season which I think it cannot possibly repeat," said Peter Wells, chief executive of Zimbabwe's Commercial Cereal Producers Association.

Wells said good weather conditions permitting, Zimbabwe looked set to produce between 300,000 and 324,000 tonnes of wheat, which is grown under irrigation in the winter month of June. That would be an increase over last season's 275,000 tonnes.
Wells expected prices to rise from their current Z$2,400 per tonne, but he would not say by how much.
